title: Babies' pauses before answering a mother grow longer around 9 months
summary: In a study of twelve pairs, infants' gaps before a vocal turn were longer at 9 and 12 months than at 5 months, while the mothers' gaps did not shift with age.
body: Hilbrink, Gattis, and Levinson measured the silence from the end of a mother's utterance to the baby's next vocalization. Infant gaps grew longer with age. Follow-up checks found the babies faster at 5 months than at 9 and at 12 months, and not reliably different at 18 months from that 5-month speed. Every infant slowed somewhere between 9 and 12 months, and eight of the twelve had their longest wait at 9 months. Separate checks found no age change in the mothers' gaps. The authors treat the slowdown as earlier than a simple first-word account predicted. Twelve pairs, and some month contrasts were exploratory, so this is one study's pattern.

sources.title: Early developmental changes in the timing of turn-taking
sources.author: Elma E. Hilbrink, Merideth Gattis, and Stephen C. Levinson
sources.note: Supports longer infant gaps at 9 and 12 months than at 5 months, no reliable maternal age effect, and the 8-of-12 slowest-at-9-months count. CC BY 4.0; paraphrased.
